newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian mob may have had hand in Albanian scams.
newsitem.headline: Italian mob may have had hand in Albanian scams.

text.p: Italian mobsters may have used Albania's failed "get-rich-quick" pyramid investment schemes to launder profits from drugs and other rackets, police and other experts said on Wednesday.

Leading anti-Mafia investigators, researchers and intelligence sources say lax controls in the impoverished former Stalinist state and the close ties between racketeers in both countries made the shady schemes a perfect home for dirty money.
"We have information that Italian crime groups were involved in Albania's financial scandal," newspapers quoted chief anti-Mafia prosecutor Pier Luigi Vigna as saying.
"Their money may have ended up in those schemes," he said.
He was echoed by the head of the Italian police organised crime squad, Alessandro Pansa, who said investigations were under way in Italy into mob links with the schemes.
Italy, a short boat trip across the Adriatic from Albania, has become a magnet for illegal immigrants from the small Balkan country since iron-fisted communist rule collapsed in 1991.
The influx has brought a substantial crime problem with it, with many of the illegals involved in prostitution, drugs and forced child labour.
Mobsters from the Puglia, Calabria and Campania regions of southern Italy have moved the other way, linking up with Albanians to traffic in drugs, arms and illegal immigrants.

"Not everyone knows that the best marijuana around today is grown just a stone's throw from Italy in Albania. The Albanians are also trying to grow coca plants," a report published this week by the Italian retailers' group Confcommercio said.
The group, which has a good record of research into Mafia money, quoted an unnamed senior police officer as saying:
"It seems that Italian organised crime groups had a hand, if not their entire arm, in the financial schemes in Tirana which have defrauded one quarter of the Albanian population," the report said.
Albania has been battered by violence and anti-government protests since the schemes began collapsing last month.
Gullible investors were initially promised monthly interest of 20 percent, with some rates rising last year to 200 percent per quarter.
Pyramid schemes flourish "mathematically" by paying interest to older investors with deposits taken from the new. The system collapses when it runs out of new customers.
Economists say up to $2 billion may have been sunk into Albania's schemes, almost as much as the gross domestic product last year in the country, Europe's poorest state.

La Repubblica newspaper quoted Vigna as saying that the sheer scale of the investments had raised suspicions about where the money came from. "We have all been a bit amazed by the size and concentration of wealth in that country," Vigna said.

An intelligence source in Rome, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said it was "quite evident" that Italian mobsters would have pumped money into the schemes early on to clean their illegal earnings and make a tidy profit into the bargain.
"It's in for the quick kill," the source said.

"If you're making money from drugs trafficking and illegal immigration and there's an opening for you to put dirty money into a system in a country where it is easier to do than in Italy, then you go for it," the source said.
